title: US DFC opens financing and risk insurance for Bangladesh private projects
excerpt: The US International Development Finance Corporation declares Bangladesh eligible for direct debt, equity and political risk insurance to support clean energy, infrastructure and technology.

image.alt: Commercial and financial towers at dusk in Dhaka, Bangladesh

content:
The United States International Development Finance Corporation (DFC) has officially declared Bangladesh eligible for its full suite of financial products and risk-mitigation tools, opening new avenues to crowd private capital into national infrastructure, renewable energy and technology sectors, officials announced on 16 November.

The decision makes commercial projects in Bangladesh eligible to compete for direct financing from the US development bank, which operates with a global investment cap of $60 billion to finance solutions in developing countries.

Instruments and eligible sectors

  • Direct debt and loan guarantees: Direct loans and guaranties up to $1 billion for terms of up to 25 years, tailored for long-gestation infrastructure and utility projects.
  • Equity investments: Direct equity and support to private equity funds investing in high-growth enterprises and financial inclusion platforms.
  • Political risk insurance: Comprehensive coverage against currency inconvertibility, regulatory expropriation, political violence and breach of sovereign contract up to $1 billion per project.
  • Priority sectors: Utility-scale renewable energy (solar, wind, grid modernization), logistics corridors, digital connectivity and micro, small and medium enterprise (MSME) lending facilities.

Eligibility criteria for project sponsors

To access DFC facilities, ventures must be commercially viable, private sector-led (or commercially operated joint ventures), and have a demonstrated developmental benefit for Bangladesh. Proposals must also comply with high environmental and social performance standards, internationally recognized worker rights and anti-corruption requirements.

Why it matters

Bangladesh faces an estimated annual infrastructure investment gap of over $20 billion, compounded by impending LDC graduation in November 2029, which will gradually restrict access to ultra-concessional multilateral loans. Access to DFC financing and political risk guarantees lowers foreign exchange and political risk premiums, making Bangladeshi infrastructure assets bankable for institutional and private international investors.

What to watch

Whether early DFC commitments focus on the government's flagship renewable energy tenders or support private banking credit lines for export-oriented green factories.
